titre: Did Eddington Cheat to Confirm Einstein in 1919?
accroche: A plate judged a failure gave almost half the expected deflection. Remeasured sixty years later, it switched sides.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 29, 1919, a total solar eclipse crosses the South Atlantic. Two British expeditions take position along its path: one at Sobral, in northern Brazil, with two astronomers from the Greenwich observatory, Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson; the other on the island of Príncipe, off the coast of West Africa, led by Arthur Eddington. The Astronomer Royal, Frank Dyson, who does not make the trip, organizes and directs the whole effort. Their instrument: photographing, during the few minutes of darkness, the stars visible close to the hidden Sun, to see whether their apparent position shifts under the effect of its gravity, as Einstein's general relativity has predicted since 1915.

## Two telescopes, three figures

Two theoretical values frame the experiment. Treated by Newtonian gravity as an ordinary mass, light should bend by 0.87 arcseconds at the edge of the Sun. Einstein's general relativity predicts double that: 1.75 arcseconds.

At Sobral, two telescopes photograph the eclipse. The first, a 4-inch lens, gives a result the report judges far superior: 1.98 arcseconds. The second, an astrographic lens, loses its focus during the eclipse, which the report attributes to the Sun's heat on the coelostat mirror; its reduction gives 0.93 arcseconds, close to the Newtonian half-value. At Príncipe, cloudy skies let Eddington photograph only five stars on two plates; his reduction method, different, gives 1.61 arcseconds, with a margin of error of 0.30.

In their 1920 report, Dyson, Eddington and Davidson set aside the astrographic value and keep the other two. The published conclusion leans clearly toward Einstein.

## The discarded figure, remeasured sixty years later

The story most often told since, popularized by a 1980 study by the philosopher of science John Earman and the physicist Clark Glymour, holds that Eddington, convinced in advance of the theory of his friend Einstein, threw out the inconvenient result so that the conclusion would come out the way he wanted: a figure close to the Newtonian half-value would have been sacrificed to his conviction.

In 1978, the Royal Observatory remeasures the original Sobral plates on a Zeiss instrument, and Geoffrey Harvey publishes the result in 1979. For the astrograph: 1.55 arcseconds, with a margin of 0.34, far from the Newtonian half-value and close to Einstein's. Harvey judges this result still weak, but it supports that of the 4-inch plates. Combined with a new measurement of the 4-inch plates (1.90, margin 0.11), his overall estimate reaches 1.87 arcseconds, within one standard deviation of Einstein's prediction.

According to Andrew Murray of the Royal Observatory, cited by Kennefick, the problem in 1919 lay less in the quality of the images than in the reduction method, which separated poorly the scale of the plates from the deflection. The historian of science Daniel Kennefick, who studied the Dyson-Eddington correspondence in 2007, also shows that the Sobral data were reduced at Greenwich, very probably without Eddington. The decision to set aside the astrograph is recorded on the data sheets in handwriting that appears to be Dyson's, and the focus defect that motivated it had been noted on site during the eclipse.

repere.texte: Remeasured in 1979 with a more precise comparator, the astrographic plates discarded in 1919 give 1.55 arcseconds (margin 0.34), against 0.93 in the original reduction: far from the Newtonian half-value of 0.87 and close to Einstein's 1.75.
repere.source: Harvey, G. M., “Gravitational Deflection of Light: A Re-examination of the Observations of the Solar Eclipse of 1919,” The Observatory, 99, 195-198, 1979

carte.punch: The plate set aside in 1919, remeasured in 1979, lands on Einstein's side
carte.idee: In 1919, the astrograph plate gave 0.93 arcseconds, almost half the deflection Einstein predicted; set aside, it fed a suspicion of cheating. Remeasured in 1979, it gives 1.55 arcseconds, close to Einstein.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Kennefick, D., “Not Only Because of Theory” (arXiv:0709.0685, 2007), full text
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The details of the Dyson-Eddington correspondence, and the 1978-1979 reanalysis of the Sobral plates.

quiz.question: Why is the value discarded in 1919 no longer seen as proof that Eddington cheated?
choix: Because Eddington publicly admitted to removing it out of personal conviction
Because a 1979 remeasurement, with a more precise comparator, gives a result close to Einstein's for that same plate
Because the 4-inch Sobral telescope later gave exactly the same value as the discarded astrographic plate
Because only the Príncipe measurement was ultimately kept in the 1920 report
quiz.explication: The astrographic plate gave 0.93'' in 1919, close to the Newtonian half-value; remeasured in 1979 with a more precise instrument, it gives 1.55'' ± 0.34'', consistent with Einstein. Kennefick establishes that the decision to set aside the astrograph is recorded in what appears to be Dyson's hand, and the 1920 report keeps two instruments, not one.
